title: Chapter 8: SQL Server on EC2: Self-Managed in the Cloud

questions.q: In a VPC, why can't an Always On availability group listener use a single floating IP across AZs, and what is the solution?
options: VPCs don't support DNS; use IP addresses directly
Security groups block floating IPs; disable them during failover
An IP cannot float across AZs because subnets are AZ-scoped — use a multi-subnet listener with MultiSubnetFailover=True in client connection strings
AG listeners are not supported on EC2 at all
questions.explain: The chapter explains the listener gets one IP per AZ subnet, DNS returns all of them, and MultiSubnetFailover=True makes the driver try all IPs in parallel — without it, clients wait out TCP timeouts on dead IPs.

questions.q: For SQL Server Enterprise licensing on EC2, an r6i.2xlarge with 8 vCPUs requires:
options: 4 core licenses, because vCPUs map to hyperthreads and SQL Server licensing counts physical cores with a 4-core minimum per VM
8 core licenses, one per vCPU
16 core licenses, two per vCPU
No licenses — EC2 includes Enterprise licensing for free
questions.explain: The chapter's per-core math: vCPUs map to hyperthreads, licensing counts physical cores, so 8 vCPUs need 4 core licenses — and you should size the VM to the license footprint.

questions.q: What is the chapter's tempdb guidance for SQL Server on EC2?
options: Keep tempdb on the same EBS volume as data files for simplicity
Use NVMe instance-store volumes or a dedicated gp3 volume for tempdb, with multiple equally-sized files — one per logical processor up to 8
Tempdb should share the log volume
Use a single tempdb data file regardless of core count
questions.explain: The chapter calls tempdb-on-shared-EBS the most common EC2 storage mistake; tempdb allocation contention shows as PAGELATCH_UP waits — give it dedicated throughput or instance-store NVMe with one file per logical processor up to 8.

questions.q: What is the correct patching order for an Always On availability group on EC2?
options: Patch the primary first, then fail over to validate
Patch all replicas simultaneously to stay in sync
Patch only the primary; secondaries inherit the patch via replication
Patch secondaries first, validate the workload on a patched readable secondary, then fail over — rollback is failing back to an unpatched secondary
questions.explain: The chapter's disciplined pattern: never patch the primary first — roll secondaries first, validate on the patched readable secondary as a canary, and keep rollback as failing back to a replica you haven't patched yet.

questions.q: Your EC2 native backups are successfully copied to S3. Per the chapter, what does this prove?
options: That the backups are restorable
That your RPO is met
Only that the copy worked — only an automated restore plus DBCC CHECKDB proves the backup is restorable
That Object Lock immutability is configured
questions.explain: The chapter warns that treating the S3 copy as backup testing is a classic mistake: the copy proves the copy worked; schedule an automated monthly restore test with DBCC CHECKDB and alert on its failure.
